lines.text: In the heart of Africa lies a land of forests and rivers, of a self-made emperor and years of war. This is the Central African Republic.
In 1889 the French set up a post on the Ubangi River. It grew into Bangui, the capital.
Around it they ruled the colony of Ubangi-Shari, leasing much of the land to companies that worked it hard.
Barthelemy Boganda, a priest, would lead the call for independence, only to die in a plane crash in 1959.
Jean-Bedel Bokassa, a soldier, would seize power in 1966, and later crown himself emperor.
David Dacko would be the first president of the new republic.
And Faustin-Archange Touadera, born in 1957, would become president in 2016.
In 1960 the colony became independent, as the Central African Republic.
In 1976 Bokassa declared an empire, and was crowned in lavish style. Three years later France removed him.
In 1990 a reserve was made in the south-west forests at Dzanga-Sangha, home to forest elephants and gorillas.
In 2012 Seleka rebels marched on Bangui, and the country fell into a war that has not fully ended.
Rich in forests and hardship alike, the Central African Republic is still searching for peace.
